claims.text: Toughness retention in HEAs is primarily governed by atomic-scale disorder that inhibits embrittling intermetallic-compound formation.
Rapid cooling from a homogenized state preserves a metastable, disordered microstructure.
The rapidly cooled disordered microstructure suppresses elemental segregation at grain boundaries and within grains.
Suppressing segregation and retaining disorder preserves toughness.
The proposed initial material is an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy produced by conventional casting and homogenization annealing.
Homogenization annealing ensures chemical uniformity in the initial alloy.
The controlled intervention is rapid quenching, such as water quenching, versus slow furnace cooling after homogenization.
The relevant structural mediators are nanoscale intermetallic precipitates and atomic-level disorder, particularly at grain boundaries.
Rapid quenching limits atomic diffusion and phase segregation.
Limited diffusion maintains a disordered solid solution and resists nucleation and growth of brittle intermetallic phases.
Slow cooling provides enough time for diffusion and elemental partitioning.
Diffusion and elemental partitioning during slow cooling lead to intermetallic-phase formation that embrittles the alloy.
Rapidly quenched samples will have greater work-to-fracture and higher impact toughness than slow-cooled samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will contain fewer or no detectable intermetallic compounds relative to slow-cooled samples.
Slow furnace cooling after homogenization is expected to cause partial embrittlement through detrimental intermetallic-phase formation.
The proposed behavior should apply to compositionally similar transition-metal HEAs, particularly the CrMnFeCoNi family, when cooling rate substantially alters diffusion kinetics.
The proposed behavior may not apply when other processing steps or compositional modifications already stabilize the disordered state.
Transformation-induced plasticity may also contribute to toughness.
Similar intermetallic precipitation in quenched and slow-cooled samples together with no statistically significant toughness improvement would falsify the proposed mechanism.
